title: The Chart That Hid the Answer
subtitle: The night before the Challenger launch, engineers argued against flying in the cold. The pattern that proved their point was in their data, but it was not in their charts.

card.essence: A long night, a dozen charts and one missing set of dots. Why the numbers never speak for themselves, and the sentence that makes them speak.

intention: you'll see why data without a meaning gets ignored, build a one-sentence 'finding, so what, now what' summary, and use it to turn a number into a clear message in under twenty seconds.
warmup: Think of a meeting where someone showed a lot of numbers. What did you remember afterwards, and what did you forget?
When you are given a report, where do you look first: the figures, the summary, or the recommendation? Why?
Have you ever been right about something and still not been believed? What was missing?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The data showed a clear correlation between the temperature on the day and the amount of damage to the seals.
items.meaning: correlation — a relationship between two things, so that when one changes the other tends to change too. It does not by itself prove that one causes the other.

items.sent: The chart omitted every flight with no damage, so the pattern disappeared.
items.meaning: omit — to leave something out, either by accident or on purpose. The noun is omission.

items.sent: Put side by side on a single page, the contrast between the two groups was stark.
items.meaning: stark — very clear and impossible to ignore, often in an uncomfortable way. A stark choice, a stark warning.

items.sent: The figures were clear, but their implications for the schedule were not.
items.meaning: implication — what something suggests or leads to, even if no one has said it directly. What are the implications of this?

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: drive home · bury the lead · the burden of proof. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means to hide the most important fact deep inside a text or talk, after less important details?
items.meaning: bury the lead — The report buried the lead: the key recommendation appeared on page eleven. Journalists spell it lede.

items.sent: Which term means the duty to show that something is true, which usually falls on the person making the claim?
items.meaning: the burden of proof — In court, the burden of proof is on the prosecution. It becomes a problem when it is quietly passed to the wrong side.

items.sent: Which term means to make a point so clearly and strongly that it cannot be missed?
items.meaning: drive home — She used one vivid example to drive the message home.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: ___ a conclusion  ·  ___ attention to a risk  ·  ___ a comparison
items.meaning: draw — draw a conclusion, draw attention to something, draw a comparison.

items.sent: convey a ___  ·  the key ___  ·  a mixed ___
items.meaning: message — the central idea you want the listener to receive. A mixed message is one that points in two directions at once.

items.sent: ___ a case  ·  ___ a difference  ·  ___ a decision
items.meaning: make — make a case (for something), make a difference, make a decision.

vocab_use: Tell me about a report or presentation where the implications were not obvious. What should the speaker have said?
Think of a news story or an email that buried the lead. Where was the real point, and how long did it take you to find it?
What is the most stark statistic you have heard recently, and what conclusion would you draw from it?

story.heading: Part 1 — The night before
paras: In January 1986 NASA was preparing to launch the space shuttle Challenger from Florida. The two solid rocket boosters were built in sections, and each joint between the sections was sealed with rubber rings called O-rings. On some earlier flights, hot gas had damaged those rings.

The boosters were built by a company called Morton Thiokol. Its engineers feared that cold weather would make the rubber stiffer and slower to seal. The forecast for the morning of 28 January was unusually cold. The coldest earlier launch had been at 53 degrees Fahrenheit, about 12 degrees Celsius, and no one had launched in anything like what was expected.
On the evening of 27 January, Thiokol engineers and managers joined NASA officials on a long teleconference. The engineers' message was simple: do not launch in these temperatures.
checks: What was used to seal the joints between the booster sections?
Why were the engineers worried about the weather?
What was the engineers' message on the evening of 27 January?
answers: They feared cold would make the rubber stiffer and slower to seal, and no launch had been anywhere near that cold.
Do not launch in these temperatures.
story.discuss: A warning is only useful if the listener understands it within the first minute. How would you test whether your own warnings can be understood that fast?

story.heading: Part 2 — The dots that were not on the page
paras: Thiokol made its case with about a dozen charts. Most of them were tables and technical detail. NASA managers were not convinced, partly because the link between cold and damage was hard to see in what they were shown.

One important chart listed only the flights on which the rings had been damaged, with the launch temperature beside each. It left out the flights with no damage at all. Without those flights the dots looked scattered, and nothing seemed to connect temperature to damage. When the investigators later plotted every flight, the pattern was clear: the worst damage had come on the coldest earlier launch.

NASA officials pushed back hard. One of them said afterwards that the meeting felt as though Thiokol had to prove beyond doubt that it was unsafe to fly, instead of NASA having to show that it was safe. After a private break, Thiokol's managers changed their recommendation.
checks: What did the important chart leave out?
What did the pattern look like once every flight was plotted?
What did Thiokol's managers do after the private break?
answers: The flights on which the rings had not been damaged.
The worst damage had come on the coldest earlier launch: the colder the launch, the greater the risk.
They changed the company's recommendation, so that it no longer advised against launching.
story.discuss: Imagine you were one of the engineers and had time to say only one sentence before the managers took their break. What would it have been?

story.heading: Part 3 — What the investigation said
paras: The shuttle was launched on the morning of 28 January. Seventy-three seconds later it broke apart, and all seven crew members were killed. The investigation, led by a presidential commission, found that a joint seal had failed in the cold.

The commission also criticised what it called a serious flaw in the decision-making process before the launch. Pressure on the schedule, the way the burden of proof had been reversed, and the way the evidence was presented all played a part. Writers still disagree about how much weight each deserves, and this lesson is only about the third.

The statistician and designer Edward Tufte later argued that the charts had hidden the argument. The evidence the room needed was in the data, but nobody could see at a glance what it proved. His lesson for speakers is simple: before you show anything, know the sentence the evidence is meant to prove, and say that sentence.
checks: What did the investigation find about the joint seal?
Besides the charts, what other factors did the commission point to?
What did Tufte say the charts failed to do?
answers: It had failed in the cold.
Pressure on the schedule and the reversal of the burden of proof, as well as the way the evidence was presented.
They did not make the argument visible: nobody could see at a glance what the data proved.
story.discuss: The engineers were right, and they were not heard in time. Is being right enough? What else does a speaker owe the listener?

tool_tab.lead: Data never speaks for itself. Someone has to say what it means, and what to do about it. Barbara Minto, who taught consultants to write and speak at McKinsey, called this answering the listener's silent question: So what? The tool below is a single sentence with three parts. Say it before you show the evidence, and the evidence becomes proof instead of noise.
how: Finding. Start from your evidence and pick the one fact that matters. Say it with one number: Response times have doubled since March.
So what. Say which means… and finish the thought. What does the finding change? …which means we are losing customers faster than we win them.
Now what. Add the ask, so that the listener knows what to do with it: So I recommend that we pause the rollout until the fault is fixed.
Test it. Imagine the listener saying So what? after your first sentence. If your sentence has not already answered that, add the meaning before you show a single chart.

sort.intro: These sentences come from the opening of a presentation. What job does each one do? Choose, then check.

items.text: Complaints rose by forty per cent after the new system went live.
items.why: a fact with one number, and nothing yet about what it means.

items.text: Which means customers are leaving faster than we can replace them.
items.why: it starts with which means and finishes the thought: what the number changes.

items.text: So I recommend that we pause the rollout until the fault is fixed.
items.why: a clear recommendation: it tells the listener what to do with the finding.

items.text: I have prepared a number of slides and I would like to take you through all of them.
items.why: it announces the format and says nothing; start with the sentence instead.

items.text: Support calls took twelve minutes on average last month.
items.why: a concrete fact with a number.

items.text: That matters because each extra minute costs us about ten thousand pounds a year.
items.why: that matters because links the fact to a consequence.

items.text: I need your approval for two extra staff by Friday.
items.why: an ask with a decision and a deadline.

items.text: As you can see on the next slide, there is quite a lot of data here.
items.why: it describes the slide instead of the message.

items.text: Which is why the problem will get worse before it gets better.
items.why: it states the implication, not the fact.

items.text: Three of our four sites missed their targets.
items.why: a fact in a short sentence, with numbers the listener can hold.

breaks: You do not know the meaning yet. Do not invent one. Say what you do know and what you do not: The finding is clear. What it means, I cannot yet say.
The link is only a possibility. One strong number does not prove a cause. Match the verb to the evidence: which suggests… rather than which proves….
The listener needs the method first. A scientific audience may want to hear how you collected the data before they accept your meaning. Even then, the best scientific papers open with the result.
discuss: Which part do you find hardest to say aloud: the finding, the meaning, or the ask? Why?
When is it better to let the listener work out the meaning for themselves?

cousins.name: The landing plan
cousins.text: The same instinct, applied to answers: point first, one reason, stop.

cousins.name: Name the Question
cousins.text: Once you know your meaning, the map of six kinds of question helps you decide what to say next.

grammar.name: Which means: linking evidence to meaning
grammar.lead: The so-what sentence depends on a handful of linking structures. The first, a comma followed by which, lets one sentence carry both the evidence and what it means.
notes: Comment clause with which: a comma plus which refers to the whole idea before it. Complaints have doubled, which means we have a serious problem. Here which stands for 'the fact that complaints have doubled'.

Other ways to link: meaning that (The test failed twice, meaning that we cannot go ahead), which is why (Costs keep rising, which is why I am asking for a review), and that matters because as a separate sentence.
Match the verb to the strength of the evidence: proves, shows, confirms are strong; suggests, points to, indicates are moderate; may mean, could indicate are cautious.

exercises.heading: Link the finding to its meaning
exercises.intro: Use each word from the box once: which · meaning · suggests · why.
items: 1. Response times have doubled, ___ means we are losing customers.
2. Only two of the nine trials worked, ___ that the method is unreliable.
3. The sample is small, which ___ that the result may not hold for everyone.
4. Costs have risen every month this year. That is ___ I am asking for a review.

exercises.heading: Match the verb to the evidence
exercises.intro: Choose the better word for the strength of the evidence.
items: 1. Every one of the 400 tests failed, which ___ (proves / suggests) the design is faulty.
2. Two of the five sites reported delays, which ___ (proves / suggests) the problem may be wider.
3. The audited accounts match the figures exactly, which ___ (confirms / hints) that the report is accurate.
4. One customer in a hundred mentioned the price, which ___ (shows / hints) that price is not the main concern.
answers: 1. proves — all 400 failed, so strong language is justified.
2. suggests — two sites out of five is not enough to prove anything.
3. confirms — the evidence is complete and checked.
4. hints — one in a hundred is weak evidence, so choose a cautious verb.

grammar.closing: Now say one finding from your work or reading this week and complete it with which means…

speak.intro: Decide the meaning, then speak. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “The finding is…” · “…which means…” · “That matters because…” · “So I recommend that we…” · “What I need from you is…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Twenty seconds
paras: A report says: Customer waiting time rose from four minutes to nine minutes in six months. Give the finding, say what it means, and make a recommendation. Twenty seconds, three sentences.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Choose your headline
paras: Pick one of these three facts and decide what it means: Staff turnover is at twenty-six per cent. / Eight of our ten largest customers have not ordered in three months. / The new product has been returned twice as often as the old one. Say your so-what sentence, then explain why you chose that meaning.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The story in sixty seconds
paras: Tell the story of the Challenger charts, but start with the so-what: what does it show about speaking? Then give one fact as evidence and say what a speaker should do.

final: The engineers had the right data and the wrong charts. Is it better to simplify your evidence so that the message is obvious, or to show everything so that nobody can say you hid something?
Can you give a so-what sentence that is wrong? What would a careful speaker add so that the listener knows how sure they are?
In your field, what is the most common way for good data to fail to persuade people?
From memory: explain the three parts of the so-what sentence in four sentences, using which means, that matters because, I recommend that and bury the lead.

practice.intro: One page of numbers to turn into messages. Pick one, take ten seconds to decide what it means, and speak for twenty. Say the finding, say what it means, and say what should happen next.
steps: Ten seconds: what does this number change? Who needs to do something about it?
Twenty seconds: the finding with one number, then which means…, then the ask.
Stop after the ask. If you are asked how do you know?, only then add the detail.

groups.title: Work and projects
groups.intro: Someone has handed you a figure and wants to know what to do about it.
questions: The project is twelve per cent over budget with half the work done.
Three of the five key staff have handed in their notice this quarter.
Only one in four customers opened the new feature.
Delivery times have fallen from nine days to four since March.
Meetings now take up almost half the working week.

groups.title: Sales and customers
groups.intro: The listener is a busy manager.
questions: Sales are up twenty per cent, but returns have doubled.
Our best customer now buys a third of what it bought last year.
Eighty per cent of complaints come from one product.
New customers cost four times as much to win as existing ones cost to keep.
The price comparison site shows us ten per cent more expensive than the next supplier.

groups.title: Health and safety
groups.intro: The meaning matters more than the detail.
questions: Waiting times in the emergency department have risen from two hours to five.
Nine out of ten accidents happen in the last hour of a shift.
Staff sickness has risen by a fifth over two winters.
Only forty per cent of employees completed the safety training.
The new procedure has halved the number of errors, but it takes twice as long.

groups.title: Money and the economy
groups.intro: Make the number mean something to a non-specialist.
questions: Prices have risen by six per cent while wages have risen by three.
The average rent now takes forty per cent of the average salary.
Our energy bill has doubled in two years.
Only one in five households has savings that would last three months.
Interest on the loan will cost us more than the equipment itself.

groups.title: Everyday life
groups.intro: A number you read or hear that makes you stop.
questions: The average person checks their phone around a hundred times a day.
Nearly half of adults say they read no books last year.
Most people think they are better than average drivers.
A city of a million people is losing ten thousand residents a year.
Global air travel doubled in twenty years.

models.q: The project is twelve per cent over budget with half the work done.
parts: Finding
We are twelve per cent over budget with half the work done.
So what
Which means that, if nothing changes, we will finish about twelve per cent over, and the contingency will not cover it.
Now what
I recommend that we cut the optional features now, and I need a decision by Friday.

models.q: Only one in four customers opened the new feature.
parts: Finding
Only one in four customers has opened the new feature.
So what
That suggests that most people either cannot find it or do not see why they would want it.
Now what
I'd like us to test a clearer button next week before we spend more on it.

models.q: Prices have risen by six per cent while wages have risen by three.
parts: Finding
Prices have risen twice as fast as wages.
So what
Which means most people are about three per cent poorer than a year ago.
Now what
That is why the pay review needs to happen this quarter, not next.

models.q: Waiting times in the emergency department have risen from two hours to five.
parts: Finding
The average wait has gone from two hours to five.
So what
Which means we now have patients waiting longer than a whole shift.
Now what
I need agreement to open the second assessment room from Monday.

models.q: Our best customer now buys a third of what it bought last year.
parts: Finding
Our biggest customer is buying a third of what it did last year.
So what
That matters because it was a fifth of our revenue, so we have lost about thirteen per cent of our income.
Now what
I recommend that I visit them this week to find out why.

models.q: Meetings now take up almost half the working week.
parts: Finding
Meetings now take up almost half the working week.
So what
Which means we only have about half the time to do the work the meetings are about.
Now what
I suggest that we drop every recurring meeting and add back only the ones people miss.

harder: Shorter: give the so-what sentence in a single sentence, using which means.
Interrupted: your partner says So what? after your finding. Answer immediately with the meaning.
Opposite meaning: give a different, honest meaning for the same number. Which is more likely, and how would you tell?
For a different listener: say it to a senior manager, then to a new colleague, then to a customer. The finding stays the same. The meaning and the ask change.
Cautious version: say the same sentence again, but change proves to suggests and add one thing you would check.
